name: Rear Naked Choke from Standing Back Control
summary: The rear naked choke from standing back control is a figure-four blood choke applied to a standing opponent, compressing both carotid arteries from harness control while threatening a simultaneous mat return to grounded back control.
description: Master the rear naked choke from standing back control in BJJ. Complete guide covering grip mechanics, finishing sequences, and defensive counters for all levels.
overview:
The rear naked choke from standing back control exploits a unique window of vulnerability that exists when the attacker has back exposure while both practitioners remain on their feet. Unlike the grounded version where hooks and mat friction provide stability, the standing variant relies on chest-to-back pressure, dynamic weight management, and the psychological pressure of vertical grappling to create finishing opportunities. The choking mechanics remain identical — compressing the carotid arteries through a figure-four arm configuration — but the setup pathway and positional management differ substantially from seated or supine back control.

From a strategic standpoint, this submission thrives on the inherent instability of standing back control. The defender must simultaneously manage balance, protect the neck, fight grips, and prevent being taken down, which overloads their defensive capacity. Skilled attackers exploit this cognitive burden by threatening the takedown to open the neck, or threatening the choke to force a defensive posture that enables the mat return. The choke can be finished standing, during the transition to the ground, or immediately after establishing grounded back control, making it a versatile weapon across the full spectrum of the standing-to-ground continuum.

At the competition level, standing back control finishes appear frequently in both gi and no-gi contexts, particularly following successful takedown entries, scramble back takes, and clinch-to-back transitions. The position rewards practitioners who understand timing windows — recognizing when the defender's hands are occupied with balance rather than neck protection — and who can thread the choking arm with precision under dynamic conditions.

injury_risks.injury: Loss of consciousness from blood choke
injury_risks.recovery_time: Immediate to 30 seconds with proper release

injury_risks.injury: Trachea damage from improper forearm placement
Carotid artery injury from excessive force
Head or spinal injury from uncontrolled fall while choke is applied standing
injury_risks.recovery_time: Variable — potential permanent injury if fall is uncontrolled

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive - 3-5 seconds minimum in training. Never snap or jerk the choke. Partner should have full awareness of pressure building. Standing application requires extra caution due to fall risk.
tap_signals: Verbal tap (say 'tap' or make any verbal sound)
Physical hand tap on opponent's body or mat
Going limp or loss of consciousness — release immediately
Any distress signal or unusual sound
release_protocol: Immediately release choking arm upon tap signal
Remove hooks and any body control grips
If standing, carefully guide partner to a controlled seated or side-lying position
Monitor consciousness and breathing for 30 seconds
If partner was unconscious, keep them lying down until fully alert and oriented
Never allow unconscious partner to stand immediately — risk of secondary fall injury
training_restrictions: Never use competition speed or intensity in drilling
Never apply the choke to the trachea or windpipe — blade of forearm must cross carotid arteries
Always ensure partner has clear tap access with both hands
Stop immediately if partner makes any distress sound
Never hold a choke past the tap for any reason
Beginners must practice with extremely slow progression only
When drilling standing, use mats and practice controlled descents to prevent fall injuries

variations_and_setups.description: From harness control, use the control arm to drag the opponent's nearest defending hand across their body while simultaneously threading the choking arm under the chin. The drag creates a momentary gap in neck defense that the choking arm exploits.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When opponent has both hands defending the neck in a static shell position

variations_and_setups.description: Drop your level as if initiating a takedown, forcing the opponent to base out with their hands. As their hands leave the neck to post or stabilize, thread the choking arm under the exposed chin before they can recover their defensive hand position.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When opponent maintains strong upright posture with disciplined hand defense

variations_and_setups.description: Initiate a controlled takedown while simultaneously threading the choking arm. The opponent's defensive focus splits between the falling sensation and the choke threat, creating an opening to lock the figure-four during the descent to the ground.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When standing finish proves difficult and opponent is defending the neck well while upright

attacker.name: from Standing Back Control Attacker
attacker.description: Learn to finish the rear naked choke from standing back control. Step-by-step guide covering arm threading, grip sequences, squeeze mechanics, and standing-to-ground transitions.
attacker.overview: Attacking the rear naked choke from standing back control requires coordinating upper body choking mechanics with dynamic balance management. Unlike the grounded version where you can settle into position, the standing variant demands that you create and exploit brief defensive windows while maintaining chest-to-back pressure against a mobile opponent. The key insight is that the standing position actually generates more finishing opportunities than most practitioners realize — the opponent must divide their attention between balance, grip defense, and fall prevention, creating gaps in neck protection that a prepared attacker can exploit with decisive arm threading and immediate structural compression.
key_principles: Maintain constant chest-to-back pressure throughout the entire choking sequence — separation kills the attack
Use the control arm to immobilize the opponent's defending hand before committing the choking arm
Thread the choking arm blade-first across the carotid arteries, never against the trachea
Time the choke entry to moments when the opponent's hands leave their neck — level changes, grip breaks, and balance corrections all create windows
Lock the figure-four behind the head, not behind the neck — head position creates the structural compression that finishes the choke
Be prepared to finish during the transition to ground — the descent often creates the best finishing window
setup_requirements: Secure seat belt or harness control with dominant chest-to-back connection established
At least partial lower body control through hooks, body triangle, or hip-level pressure compromising opponent's base
Identify which side the choking arm will attack from based on harness grip configuration
Confirm opponent's defensive hand positioning to plan the arm threading pathway

execution_steps.description: Lock the seat belt grip tight with one arm over the shoulder and one under the armpit. Drive your chest into the opponent's upper back and walk your hips close to eliminate any gap. Confirm your hooks or lower body control is engaged to prevent immediate separation.

Use the control arm (underhook side) to strip or redirect the opponent's nearest defending hand away from their neck. Drag their wrist across their body or pin it to their chest using two-on-one control momentarily. This creates the gap your choking arm needs to thread.

execution_steps.action: Thread the choking arm under the chin
execution_steps.description: Slide the choking arm (overhook side) under the opponent's chin with the blade of your forearm crossing both carotid arteries. The forearm should sit in the groove between the chin and the collarbone. Keep your elbow centered on their sternum, not off to one side.

execution_steps.action: Secure the figure-four lock behind the head
execution_steps.description: Place your choking hand on the bicep of your free arm. Bring your free hand behind the opponent's head and press it forward into the choking forearm. The lock should feel structural — your arms form a closed triangle around the neck with the head acting as a wedge.

Expand your chest and squeeze your elbows together using your back muscles rather than pulling with arm strength. The compression comes from the structural closing of the figure-four. Keep your hips tight against the opponent to prevent them from creating downward space to escape.

If the opponent drops their weight or the finish is not immediate, follow them to the ground while maintaining the choking grip. Establish hooks during the descent and continue the squeeze from grounded back control. The transition often tightens the choke as the opponent's defensive options decrease with the mat behind them.

common_counters.counter: Two-on-one grip strip on choking arm
common_counters.your_response: Switch to the opposite side or use the control arm to re-clear their hands. If they commit both hands to grip fighting, threaten a takedown to force them to post, then re-attack the neck when their hands leave.

common_counters.counter: Chin tuck and shoulder shrug shell defense
common_counters.your_response: Attack the jawline by threading the forearm along the mandible rather than fighting to go under the chin directly. Apply pressure to the jaw which forces the chin up, or use the knuckle of the index finger as a wedge along the jawline to create the gap.

common_counters.counter: Hip turn and facing attempt to recover clinch
common_counters.your_response: Follow the rotation by circling with the opponent while tightening harness control. If they complete a partial turn, switch to front headlock or arm triangle threat rather than fighting against their momentum to maintain back position.

common_counters.counter: Drop to knees and turtle defense
common_counters.your_response: Follow them to the ground maintaining the choking grip. The descent typically creates a tighter squeeze as the opponent compresses downward. Establish hooks immediately and finish from grounded back control where their escape options are reduced.

common_errors.error: Reaching for the choke before clearing the defending hands
common_errors.consequence: Opponent catches and strips the choking arm with two-on-one defense, resetting the attack and potentially creating space to escape back control entirely
common_errors.correction: Always use the control arm to drag or redirect the nearest defending hand before committing the choking arm. The sequence is clear-thread-lock, never thread-then-fight.

common_errors.error: Placing forearm across the trachea instead of the carotid arteries
common_errors.consequence: Creates a windpipe crush rather than a blood choke — extremely dangerous, causes pain without clean submission, and risks serious tracheal injury in training
common_errors.correction: Position the blade of the forearm in the groove between chin and collarbone, centered over the carotid arteries. The elbow should be aligned with the opponent's sternum, ensuring bilateral arterial compression.

common_errors.error: Squeezing with arm strength instead of structural compression
common_errors.consequence: Arms fatigue rapidly, the choke becomes loose under resistance, and the opponent gains time to work defensive grip strips or positional escapes
common_errors.correction: Expand your chest and squeeze elbows together using back muscles. The figure-four structure does the work — your arms maintain the shape while your torso provides the compressive force.

common_errors.error: Losing chest-to-back connection during the arm threading sequence
common_errors.consequence: Creates separation that allows the opponent to turn, drop, or create angles to escape back exposure before the choke is locked
common_errors.correction: Maintain constant chest pressure throughout the entire threading sequence. Your hips stay tight and your weight stays on the opponent's back — the arms work independently of the body connection.

common_errors.error: Locking the figure-four behind the neck instead of behind the head
common_errors.consequence: The choke lacks structural compression — the opponent can pull the choking arm down since there is no head block forcing their neck into the forearm
common_errors.correction: Place the free hand behind the crown of the head and press forward. The head acts as a wedge that drives the neck into the choking forearm, creating a closed system the opponent cannot pull out of.

common_errors.error: Fighting to keep the opponent standing when they actively drop their weight
common_errors.consequence: You fight against gravity while the opponent uses the descent to create separation, often ending with lost back control or an uncontrolled scramble
common_errors.correction: Follow the descent and maintain your grips. The transition to ground typically tightens the choke. Fighting to keep them standing wastes energy and risks losing the position entirely.

training_progressions.description: Partner stands still with no resistance. Practice threading the choking arm from harness position, locking the figure-four, and applying slow progressive pressure. Focus on forearm angle across the carotid arteries and hand placement behind the head. 20 repetitions each side.

Partner defends with both hands on their neck in shell position. Practice clearing hands with drag, redirect, and two-on-one techniques before threading the choking arm. Introduce light resistance on the hand fighting. 15 repetitions focusing on timing the thread after the clear.

Partner moves and shifts weight as in a live scramble. Practice timing the choke entry to moments when the opponent's hands leave the neck — during level changes, direction shifts, and grip adjustments. Partner at 50% resistance. 10 repetitions with increasing movement speed.

Partner actively resists standing and drops to ground. Practice maintaining the choking grip during the transition, establishing hooks on landing, and completing the finish from grounded back control. Full resistance flow drilling. 5-minute rounds alternating partners.

Start from established standing back control with harness grip. Attacker works to finish the RNC, defender works full-resistance escapes. 2-minute rounds, reset on submission or complete escape. Focus on recognizing and exploiting real-time defensive windows.

flashcards.question: What anatomical structures does the rear naked choke compress to cause the tap?
flashcards.answer: The rear naked choke compresses both carotid arteries using the blade of the choking forearm on one side and the bicep of the locking arm on the other. This bilateral compression restricts blood flow to the brain, causing rapid loss of consciousness within 4-10 seconds of a properly locked choke. The trachea should remain in the pocket created by the crook of the elbow and should not receive direct pressure.

flashcards.question: Your opponent tucks their chin tightly and you cannot thread your forearm under — what adjustment creates the opening?
flashcards.answer: Thread the forearm along the jawline rather than fighting to go under the chin directly. Apply pressure to the mandible which forces the chin upward and creates the gap. Alternatively, use the knuckle of your index finger as a wedge along the jaw line to create space. You can also threaten a level change or takedown to force their hands away from their neck, then thread when the chin lifts reactively during the balance adjustment.

flashcards.question: What are the key differences between finishing the choke standing versus following the opponent to the ground?
flashcards.answer: Standing finishes rely on dynamic balance management and exploiting brief defensive windows while the opponent's hands are occupied with balance. Ground finishes provide stability through mat friction and hooks, allowing a more patient squeeze. The standing position gives less time but more defensive overload opportunities. Most high-level finishes occur during the transition — the descent splits the opponent's attention between fall protection and choke defense, creating the best window to complete the lock.

flashcards.question: What indicators tell you the choke is properly positioned on the carotid arteries rather than the trachea?
flashcards.answer: A properly positioned blood choke produces steady bilateral pressure without significant pain complaints from the training partner. The opponent will feel lightheaded and their vision may narrow before feeling unable to breathe. If the opponent reports sharp pain in the throat, coughs, or gags, the forearm is likely on the trachea. The elbow should be centered on the sternum with the forearm blade sitting in the soft tissue lateral to the windpipe on the choking side.

flashcards.question: Why must the figure-four lock be positioned behind the head rather than behind the neck?
flashcards.answer: The hand behind the head acts as a wedge that pushes the opponent's head forward into the choking forearm, creating a closed structural system. When locked behind the neck instead, the opponent can pull the choking arm downward because there is no counterpressure driving their neck into the forearm. The head-behind position makes the choke self-tightening — any defensive movement pushes the neck deeper into the compression rather than creating escape angles.

flashcards.question: Your opponent starts to turn their shoulders explosively while you have the harness but no choke locked — how do you respond?
flashcards.answer: Follow the rotation by circling with the opponent while maintaining chest-to-back connection and harness grip. Do not fight their momentum head-on. If they complete a partial turn and you lose back angle, transition to a front headlock or arm triangle setup rather than forcing back control against their rotation. If they only turn slightly, use the momentum to take them down and establish grounded back control where their rotation options are limited by the mat.

flashcards.question: How should you release the choke immediately after your partner taps during standing training?
flashcards.answer: Release the choking arm instantly upon feeling or hearing the tap. Remove all body control grips and hooks. Because you are standing, carefully guide your partner to a controlled seated or side-lying position rather than simply releasing them to stumble. Monitor their consciousness and breathing for 30 seconds. If they lost consciousness at any point, keep them lying down until fully alert and oriented. Never allow an unconscious partner to stand — the risk of secondary fall injury is significant.

flashcards.question: What is the correct squeezing mechanic that produces efficient compression without rapid arm fatigue?
flashcards.answer: The squeeze comes from expanding your chest and squeezing your elbows toward each other using your back muscles, not from pulling with your biceps. Your arms maintain the structural shape of the figure-four while your torso provides the compressive force. Think of making your chest bigger rather than pulling your arms tighter. This uses larger, more fatigue-resistant muscle groups and produces a structural compression that the opponent cannot simply muscle out of.

flashcards.question: At what point during the standing RNC sequence does the opponent reach the point of no escape?
flashcards.answer: The point of no escape occurs when the figure-four is locked behind the head with the choking forearm correctly positioned across both carotid arteries. Before the lock is completed, the defender can still strip the choking arm with two-on-one grip fighting. Once the hand is placed behind the head and the structural triangle is closed, the defender's only realistic option is to tap. The window between threading the arm under the chin and completing the figure-four lock is the critical race — attackers must minimize this transition time while defenders must exploit it.

flashcards.question: How do you adjust your grip sequence when the opponent peels your choking hand off their bicep before the figure-four is fully locked?
flashcards.answer: If they strip the hand-to-bicep connection, immediately switch to a short choke by grabbing your own forearm or wrist instead of the bicep, maintaining forearm pressure across the neck. Alternatively, use a gable grip behind the head for a modified finish. The key is to never release the forearm from the neck position while transitioning grips — the blade stays on the arteries while only the locking configuration changes. Releasing the forearm to re-attempt the bicep grip resets the entire attack and gives the defender time to rebuild their shell.

flashcards.question: In competition, when should you commit to finishing the choke standing versus deliberately taking your opponent down first?
flashcards.answer: Commit to the standing finish when you have the figure-four locked or nearly locked and the opponent's defensive hands are already defeated. Take them down first when you have strong harness control but cannot clear the defending hands, or when the opponent's base is compromised and a controlled descent will tighten your existing grips. The worst competition decision is attempting a standing finish with an unlocked choke against an opponent with active hand defense — this burns time and energy. Use the takedown as a submission setup rather than treating standing and ground finishes as separate strategies.

defender.name: from Standing Back Control Defender
defender.description: Learn to defend and escape the rear naked choke from standing back control. Covers recognition cues, grip fighting, escape sequences, and safe tapping protocols.
defender.overview: Defending the rear naked choke from standing back control is one of the most urgent defensive scenarios in grappling. The standing position compounds the danger because you must simultaneously protect your neck, maintain balance, and prevent forceful takedowns while your attacker has structural advantages behind you. The primary survival principle is straightforward — your hands must stay on your neck until the immediate choke threat is neutralized. Every other defensive action is secondary to preventing the choking arm from threading under your chin and locking the figure-four configuration that produces bilateral carotid compression.
key_principles: Protect the neck first and always — both hands create a defensive shell before any escape attempt begins
Tuck the chin to the chest and turn slightly toward the choking arm side to close the gap
Fight the choking arm with two-on-one grip control, never let it slide under your chin unchallenged
Create space through hip movement and direction changes that exploit the inherent instability of standing
Address the harness grip systematically — reduce control points before attempting major positional escapes
If escape is not immediately available, control the descent to turtle or guard rather than being taken down on the attacker's terms
recognition_cues: Opponent transitions their overhook arm from shoulder control toward your chin or jawline — the choking arm is being positioned for the thread
Feeling the harness grip shift as the control arm begins dragging your defending hand away from your neck to create an opening
Opponent's chest pressure increases and hooks tighten simultaneously, indicating they are consolidating position before committing to the choke attempt
Opponent adjusts their head position to the choking side and their breathing pattern changes, indicating commitment to the finish

defensive_options.action: Two-on-one grip strip on the choking arm
defensive_options.when_to_use: As soon as you feel the choking arm begin to thread under your chin or along your jawline
defensive_options.if_successful: Resets the choke attempt and forces the attacker to re-clear your hands before trying again
defensive_options.risk: Both hands on the choking arm temporarily leaves you vulnerable to takedowns and position changes

defensive_options.action: Chin tuck with shoulder shrug shell defense
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the choking arm is approaching but has not yet threaded under the chin — preventive posture
defensive_options.if_successful: Blocks the forearm from reaching the carotid arteries, buying time for grip fighting and escape work
defensive_options.risk: Static defense that only delays the attack — must be combined with active grip fighting to create escape

defensive_options.action: Hip turn and face the attacker
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the attacker's lower body control is weak — no hooks or only one hook engaged
defensive_options.if_successful: Eliminates back exposure entirely, transitions to clinch or guard position
defensive_options.risk: If harness grip is still strong, the turn can tighten the choke rather than create escape

defensive_options.when_to_use: When standing defense is failing and the choke is partially locked — change the angle to buy time
defensive_options.if_successful: Changes the angle of attack, provides the mat as a defensive surface, and opens turtle escape sequences
defensive_options.risk: Opponent may follow to grounded back control with stronger finishing position

escape_paths: Two-on-one grip strip to hip turn and face the attacker, recovering to clinch or neutral standing position
Controlled descent to turtle with immediate escape sequences to half guard or neutral position
Peel the choking arm and duck under to reverse the position or recover to neutral standing

favorable_outcomes.how: Successfully strip the harness grip, turn to face the opponent, and pull them into your closed guard during the resulting scramble. This requires defeating the choking arm first, then using an explosive hip turn when the attacker's hooks are not fully engaged.

common_errors.error: Reaching behind to push the attacker's head or body instead of defending the neck
common_errors.consequence: Exposes the neck completely — the choking arm threads under the chin while your hands are behind you rather than protecting the target area
common_errors.correction: Keep both hands on your neck in the defensive shell position. Fight the choking arm with two-on-one control. Never reach behind — your hands should only leave your neck to strip the choking arm directly.

common_errors.error: Panicking and making wild explosive movements to escape
common_errors.consequence: Burns energy rapidly, creates unpredictable momentum the attacker can exploit, and often results in falling with the choke partially locked
common_errors.correction: Stay calm and work the systematic defensive sequence: protect neck, fight grips, create angle, execute escape. Controlled technical movement is far more effective than explosive panic under pressure.

common_errors.error: Pulling the choking arm downward away from the neck rather than stripping it laterally
common_errors.consequence: Pulling the arm downward can actually help the attacker seat the forearm deeper across the carotid arteries by feeding the neck into the blade of the forearm
common_errors.correction: Strip the choking arm by pushing it toward your chin and over the top of your head, or use two-on-one to peel it laterally away from the neck. The direction of your grip strip matters — move the arm away from the arteries, not across them.

common_errors.error: Attempting to turn into the attacker while the harness grip is still locked tight
common_errors.consequence: The turn tightens the harness and can help the attacker lock the choking arm as your rotation feeds your neck into the forearm
common_errors.correction: Break or significantly loosen the harness grip before attempting any major turning escape. The sequence is strip grips first, then create angle, then turn to face.

flashcards.question: What is the absolute first priority when you feel the choking arm threading under your chin?
flashcards.answer: Immediately use both hands to grab the choking arm wrist and forearm with a two-on-one grip, pulling it away from your neck before the figure-four can be locked. Simultaneously tuck your chin as tightly as possible to your chest. Once the figure-four is locked behind your head, escape becomes dramatically more difficult, so the window to stop the threading arm is the critical moment.

flashcards.question: When should you tap to a rear naked choke rather than continuing to fight the escape?
flashcards.answer: Tap immediately when you feel the figure-four locked behind your head and bilateral pressure on both carotid arteries, or when you notice any vision changes such as tunnel vision or darkening. In training, there is no benefit to fighting a fully locked blood choke — loss of consciousness occurs within 4-10 seconds and continuing to fight risks going unconscious without tapping. Tap early, learn from the positional failure, and drill the earlier defensive windows.

flashcards.question: Why is controlling your descent to the ground often a better defensive strategy than fighting to stay standing?
flashcards.answer: Dropping to turtle or guard on your own terms changes the angle of the choke attack, provides the mat as an additional defensive surface, and opens escape sequences unavailable while standing. Fighting to stay standing while the choke is being set up divides your attention between balance and neck defense, making both worse. A controlled descent also prevents the attacker from slamming or forcefully taking you down, which could compound the danger of a partially locked choke.

flashcards.question: What defensive hand position should you maintain before beginning any escape attempt?
flashcards.answer: Both hands should form a defensive shell around your neck — one hand controls the opponent's choking arm wrist, the other hand cups your own neck or reinforces the grip on the choking arm. Your chin is tucked tightly to your chest. This shell must remain in place until you actively strip the choking arm. Removing your hands to attempt escapes, push the opponent away, or grab their legs exposes your neck to the finish and should never be done before neutralizing the choke threat.

flashcards.question: How does the standing variant change your defensive urgency compared to ground-based rear naked choke defense?
flashcards.answer: The standing variant increases urgency because you face simultaneous threats — the choke itself, loss of balance, and the risk of falling while the choke is partially locked. Unlike ground defense where you can use the mat for leverage and frames, standing defense relies almost entirely on grip fighting and hip movement. However, the standing position also creates opportunity: the inherent instability means the attacker's control is less secure, and explosive direction changes can create separation impossible when the attacker has hooks and mat pressure.

flashcards.question: Your attacker has threaded the choking arm deep and is reaching for their bicep to lock the figure-four — what is your last window of defense?
flashcards.answer: This is the final critical window before the choke becomes structurally locked. Use both hands to attack the wrist of the choking arm, pulling it away from the bicep connection point. Simultaneously shrug your near shoulder up into the crook of the choking arm elbow to create space and reduce arterial compression. If you cannot prevent the hand-to-bicep connection within 1-2 seconds, immediately initiate a controlled drop while continuing to fight the grip — the angle change during descent may create enough slack to prevent the full lock.

flashcards.question: What is the correct direction to strip the choking arm once it has threaded under your chin but the figure-four is not yet locked?
flashcards.answer: Strip the choking arm upward toward your chin and over the top of your head, or peel it laterally away from the side of your neck using two-on-one control. Never pull the forearm downward toward your chest, as this motion drags the blade of the forearm across the carotid arteries and can actually deepen the choke. The stripping direction must move the forearm away from the arterial targets, not across them. Think of peeling the arm off like removing a scarf over your head rather than pulling it down around your neck.

flashcards.question: How should you recognize the difference between a blood choke that requires an immediate tap and a discomforting but survivable jaw or neck crank?
flashcards.answer: A properly applied blood choke produces a sensation of lightheadedness, visual narrowing or tunnel vision, and a feeling of fading consciousness without necessarily causing sharp pain. A jaw crank or neck crank produces localized pain in the jaw, teeth, or cervical spine without the lightheadedness. However, in training you should tap to both — a crank can cause injury and a choke can render you unconscious within seconds. The distinction matters for defensive positioning: against a blood choke, immediate grip stripping is paramount; against a crank, adjusting head angle can relieve pressure while you work the escape.

training_progressions.phase: Phase 1: Shell Defense and Tap Recognition
training_progressions.focus: Building the defensive hand position and recognizing when to tap
training_progressions.description: Partner slowly applies the RNC from standing back control. Practice maintaining the defensive shell, identifying when the choke is locked versus when it can still be defended. Tap at appropriate moments. Focus on calm breathing and pressure awareness rather than escape. 20 slow repetitions.

training_progressions.focus: Two-on-one grip strips and hand fighting sequences
training_progressions.description: Partner attempts to thread the choking arm at moderate resistance. Practice the timing and mechanics of two-on-one grip strips, redirecting the choking arm, and resetting the defensive shell after each strip. 15 repetitions per side focusing on grip strip direction and timing.

training_progressions.focus: Full escape paths from grip strip to positional recovery
training_progressions.description: Partner applies standing back control with RNC intent at 50-75% resistance. Practice full escape chains: shell defense to grip strip to hip turn and face, and shell defense to controlled descent to turtle to guard recovery. 10 repetitions of each pathway with increasing resistance.

training_progressions.focus: Real-time defensive decision making under full pressure
training_progressions.description: Full resistance positional rounds starting from standing back control. Defender works to escape or neutralize the choke, attacker works for the finish. 2-minute rounds resetting on submission or complete escape. Focus on applying the defensive sequence under genuine pressure while maintaining composure and recognizing tap moments.
